script.opening: "My wife made me come — honestly I think it’s a fuss over nothing. Yesterday my right arm went weak and my words came out slurred for maybe half an hour, then it cleared up completely and I’ve been fine since. So no harm done, right? I don’t need to do anything about it now it’s passed?"

facts.text: Yesterday about 4 pm, sitting reading the paper. "My right hand just went useless — I dropped my mug, couldn’t lift the arm properly." At the same time "my words came out mushy". His wife said the right side of his mouth looked "a bit droopy". It came on suddenly, all at once.
"Half an hour, maybe a bit less." Then everything came back completely. If asked: no weakness, numbness or speech trouble now. "I feel absolutely fine today."

No headache, no loss of consciousness, no fit or jerking, no vision loss in one eye ("no curtain coming down"), no double vision, no chest pain. Has noticed his heart "fluttering" once or twice in the last few months but put it down to coffee.
Never had anything like it before. If asked directly: "Now you mention it, a couple of weeks ago my right hand went tingly and clumsy for a few minutes, but I ignored it."

High blood pressure for about 10 years — "on one tablet, I can’t remember the name". Doesn’t check his blood pressure at home. No diabetes he knows of; cholesterol "a bit high once". Not on aspirin or blood thinners. No allergies. No stomach ulcers or bleeding problems.

Ex-smoker — 20 a day for 30 years, stopped 8 years ago. Drinks "a couple of pints at the weekend". Retired bus mechanic. Lives with his wife, Pat. Drives a car every day (no HGV or bus licence now). Has aspirin "in the cupboard somewhere".
Father died of a stroke at 72. Brother had a heart attack in his sixties.
Due to drive to his daughter’s in Leeds on Saturday (about two hours) to babysit the grandchildren. If told he can’t drive: "Nobody’s ever told me that. I suppose I can get a lift."

Relaxed and a bit dismissive at first; slightly embarrassed his wife made him book. If the doctor explains clearly and kindly that this was a warning of a stroke, go quiet, then admit the fear (see concerns). If the doctor just reassures you, accept it happily. Agree to aspirin and the clinic if it is explained; push back mildly on not driving.

ice.ideas: "It came and went, so it can’t have been anything serious. Maybe I slept funny on the arm, or it was a trapped nerve."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — only if explored: "I suppose I did think it was a stroke at the time. Dad had one and was never the same — he couldn’t talk properly for his last two years. When it went away I told myself I’d imagined it." He minimises because he is frightened.
ice.expectations: "For you to tell me it’s fine so my wife stops worrying." Not expecting tests or medicine, and has no idea it affects driving.

cues: "My wife made me come" — he would not have booked himself; the minimising is a defence.
"So no harm done, right?" — invites false reassurance; the candidate must explain this is an emergency warning of stroke.
"I’m driving up to my daughter’s on Saturday" (if driving or plans are asked about) — the opening for the no-driving advice.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a transient, fully-resolving FOCAL neurological deficit as a TIA — a MEDICAL EMERGENCY and stroke warning — and that full recovery does NOT mean "no harm done"

Takes a focused history (deficit type/onset/duration/resolution, FAST, amaurosis fugax, palpitations/AF, vascular risk) and arranges a same-day face-to-face examination (BP, pulse/rhythm, carotids, neuro confirming resolution, CVS — not possible by video), considering mimics

Gives ASPIRIN 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated/anticoagulated) and refers for SPECIALIST TIA assessment within 24 HOURS of onset per NICE NG128 (no ABCD2-based selective delay; no CT unless an alternative diagnosis is suspected)

Knows the secondary-prevention package (antiplatelet — usually long-term clopidogrel — or anticoagulation if AF, high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg, NICE NG238), BP control to systolic below 130 mmHg, smoking cessation, diabetes, carotid surgery if significant symptomatic stenosis)

Advises he MUST NOT DRIVE — Group 1 no driving for 1 month (multiple TIAs: 3 months attack-free and notify DVLA; notify if residual deficit), Group 2 must stop, notify DVLA and wait 1 year for relicensing — and documents the advice
Firmly but supportively corrects the "no harm done/it’s passed" minimisation, conveys the urgency and the prevention opportunity, and validates the wife’s prompt
Explains the reasoning (resolved = warning to act now) in accessible terms and checks understanding

Safety-nets and arranges disposition: aspirin started, within-24h specialist assessment, 999 advice if any new/persistent deficit (FAST), no driving, and review — acting on a resolved TIA as an emergency, not reassurance

worked.txt: "Your wife was absolutely right to make you come — and I have to be honest with you: the fact it cleared up is not ‘no harm done’. What you describe is a mini-stroke, a TIA, and it’s a serious warning that a bigger stroke could follow, especially in the next few days. That’s exactly why we act now."

"Tell me again — which side, how long, did it fully clear? Any change in vision, palpitations? I can watch your speech and face on video, but I can’t check your blood pressure or pulse — an irregular pulse matters — or do a proper neurological check this way, so that examination will be done face to face today at the TIA clinic."

"Two things now: I’m giving you aspirin 300 mg today, and I’m arranging for you to be seen by the stroke/TIA specialists within 24 hours — they’ll examine you, scan the neck arteries, decide whether you need a brain scan, and sort out prevention. This isn’t something to leave."

"The good news is a TIA is a treatable warning — blood-pressure control, a statin, stopping smoking, and treating any irregular heartbeat dramatically cut your stroke risk. We turn this into a near-miss, not a disaster."

"Important: you must not drive for now — after a TIA that’s a month for a car, and if you drive a bus or lorry you must stop, tell the DVLA, and it’s a year before you can be relicensed. I know that’s inconvenient, but it’s the law and it’s for your safety. I’ll document it."

"If any weakness, droopy face, or slurred speech comes back and stays — even briefly — call 999 immediately; that could be a stroke and time is critical. Otherwise, expect the specialist contact within a day, and I’ll follow up."

f.learning: A transient, fully-resolving FOCAL neurological deficit of presumed vascular origin (unilateral weakness, dysarthria/dysphasia, facial droop, amaurosis fugax) is a TRANSIENT ISCHAEMIC ATTACK — and full recovery does NOT mean "no harm done": a TIA is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY and a strong warning of imminent stroke (risk highest in the first days), so the resolution is precisely why it must be acted on urgently. Take a focused history (deficit type/onset/duration/complete resolution, FAST features, amaurosis fugax, palpitations suggesting AF, prior episodes, vascular risk) and arrange a same-day face-to-face examination, which video cannot provide (BP, pulse/rhythm for AF, carotids, a neuro exam confirming resolution, CVS), considering mimics (hypoglycaemia, seizure with Todd’s paresis, migraine aura, syncope) but treating as TIA until excluded. Give ASPIRIN 300 mg immediately (unless contraindicated or already anticoagulated, per local pathway) and refer immediately for SPECIALIST TIA-clinic assessment within 24 HOURS of onset — NICE NG128 says do not use scoring systems such as ABCD2 to decide urgency — for carotid imaging, specialist-decided brain imaging (no CT unless an alternative diagnosis that CT could detect is suspected), ECG, bloods and secondary prevention (antiplatelet — long-term clopidogrel in most — or anticoagulation if AF, NICE NG196; atorvastatin 80 mg, NICE NG238; BP control to systolic below 130 mmHg, smoking cessation, diabetes optimisation, carotid endarterectomy if significant symptomatic stenosis), reframing the TIA as a treatable warning. Critically, advise the patient MUST NOT DRIVE: Group 1 (car) 1 month off (multiple TIAs over a short period: 3 months attack-free with DVLA notification; notify if residual deficit), Group 2 (HGV/bus) must stop, notify DVLA and wait 1 year for relicensing — advise clearly and document. The hidden agenda is minimisation ("it’s passed, no harm done", attending only at his wife’s insistence); firmly but supportively correct it, convey urgency and the prevention opportunity, and never be reassured by the recovery.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG128 (stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management, 2019, updated 2022) · [2] National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland (ICSWP, 2023) · [3] NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · [4] NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation, 2021) · [5] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition) · [6] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017)
knowledge.summary: Sudden right arm weakness with slurred speech lasting about 30 minutes and fully resolving, in a 69-year-old hypertensive ex-smoker, is a suspected TIA until a specialist says otherwise. Recovery is the reason to act, not a reason to relax: the stroke risk is highest in the first days. The GP’s job is aspirin 300 mg now unless contraindicated, a same-day referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset, clear no-driving advice and a firm 999 safety net.

points.t: A sudden focal deficit (unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, facial droop, monocular visual loss) that fully resolves is a suspected TIA. Arm weakness plus dysarthria or dysphasia points to the anterior circulation. Mimics — hypoglycaemia, focal seizure with Todd’s paresis, migraine aura, syncope — are considered, but the default is to treat as TIA [1].

NICE NG128 [1]: offer aspirin 300 mg immediately to people with suspected TIA unless contraindicated. If he already takes an anticoagulant, or has a bleeding disorder or aspirin hypersensitivity, do not give it and discuss with the TIA service [1].

NICE NG128 [1]: refer immediately to be seen by a stroke specialist within 24 hours of symptom onset. If the TIA was more than a week ago, the target is within 7 days. NG128 says do not use scoring systems such as ABCD2 to decide urgency — every suspected TIA gets the urgent route. Symptoms that return and persist mean 999, not the clinic.

NICE NG128 [1]: do not offer CT brain to people with suspected TIA unless an alternative diagnosis that CT could detect is suspected. The specialist decides on MRI (diffusion-weighted) and arranges urgent carotid imaging. Carotid endarterectomy is considered for 50–99% symptomatic stenosis (NASCET), ideally within a week of onset.

Delivered by the TIA service and continued in general practice: long-term clopidogrel in most people, with short specialist-started dual antiplatelet therapy for selected high-risk TIA [2]; anticoagulation instead if AF is found (NICE NG196 [4]); atorvastatin 80 mg unless there is a reason for a lower dose (NICE NG238 [3]); blood pressure target of systolic below 130 mmHg [2]; staying off tobacco; diabetes and lipid checks.

DVLA [5]: Group 1 (car, motorcycle) — must not drive for 1 month. No need to notify DVLA if fully recovered at 1 month with no residual deficit. After multiple TIAs, the 1-month exclusion applies after each episode; notify DVLA where the current guidance requires. Group 2 (bus, coach, lorry): stop driving and notify; relicensing needs 1 year. Record the advice in the notes [6].

On video you can watch speech and face and ask about symptoms, but you cannot take a blood pressure, feel the pulse for AF or listen for a bruit. Say so, and make sure the TIA clinic does the examination, ECG and bloods the same day.
‘It’s passed, so no harm done’ is a common reason for dangerous delay. Name it kindly, credit the person who pushed him to come, and explain that the warning is the chance to prevent a stroke.

dg.d: Open question; let him give the full story and his ‘no harm done’ view before questioning.
Acknowledged the wife’s role; explored his fear of stroke; asked about driving and who could take him to clinic.
Used video to observe speech, face and arm drift; stated that BP, pulse, bruits, ECG and bloods need the TIA clinic today.
Considered mimics (hypoglycaemia, seizure, migraine aura, syncope) and amaurosis fugax; kept TIA as the working diagnosis.
Checked for persisting deficit (999 if present) and for anticoagulant, bleeding risk and aspirin allergy.
Suspected anterior-circulation TIA; explained as a mini-stroke and a warning with the highest risk in the next few days.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Aspirin 300 mg now; immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset; no ABCD2 triage; outlined clopidogrel, statin, BP and AF plan.
Linked hypertension and smoking history to prevention; AF to be sought; driving advice with DVLA rules documented.
999 for any recurrence; chase the clinic if no call today; review after clinic; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up ‘it’s passed’ as minimisation and the hidden fear behind it; explored rather than argued.
Idea: resolved means harmless. Concern: unspoken fear of stroke. Expectation: permission to ignore it.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — only if explored: "I suppose I did think it was a stroke at the time. Dad had one and was never the same — he couldn’t talk properly for his last two years. When it went away I told myself I’d imagined it." He minimises because he is frightened — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Cole, I’m Dr Ahmed. Thank you for joining the video call. Can I just check you’re somewhere private, and that I can see and hear you clearly? What’s been happening?
model.why: Confirms the video set-up and opens with an open question

model.text: Yes, I’m at home. My wife made me book, to be honest. Yesterday my right arm went weak and my words came out slurred for maybe half an hour, then it cleared up completely. So no harm done, is there? I don’t need to do anything now it’s passed?
I’m really glad your wife pushed you, and I want to take this seriously with you. Can I ask a few quick questions about exactly what happened, and then tell you honestly what I think?
model.why: Validates the wife’s prompt and sets a clear, brief agenda

model.text: Go on then.
When it started, was it sudden? And was it only the right arm, or the face or leg too? When you say slurred — was it that your words were thick, or that you couldn’t find or understand the words?
model.why: Characterises onset, distribution and type of speech disturbance

model.text: Sudden. Just the arm, I think. My words sounded wrong. It all came back after about half an hour.
Has it gone completely — the arm strong, the speech normal, no numbness left? Any loss of vision in one eye, double vision, headache, or jerking before or after?
model.why: Confirms full resolution; screens for amaurosis fugax and mimics such as seizure or migraine

model.text: All back to normal. No headache or anything like that.

Your speech sounds clear to me now, and your face looks even on the screen. Could you hold both arms straight out in front of you with your eyes closed for ten seconds? … That looks steady. I can’t check your pulse or blood pressure over video, so the clinic will do that today.
model.why: Uses what video allows and names what it cannot do

model.text: Right.
Have you had anything like this before? Any fluttering or racing heartbeat? And do you take any blood thinners, or have any problem with aspirin or bleeding?
model.why: Asks about previous episodes, symptoms of AF and aspirin contraindications

model.text: Nothing like that. Just my blood pressure tablets.
You said ‘no harm done’. What went through your mind while it was happening?
model.why: Explores the fear behind the minimisation

model.text: (pause) I suppose I thought it was a stroke. Then it went, so I told myself I’d imagined it.
That must have been frightening, and it’s very human to want it to be nothing. Thank you for telling me.
model.why: Acknowledges the unspoken fear with empathy

model.text: I think this was a TIA — a mini-stroke. A blood vessel to the brain was briefly blocked, then cleared. The fact it cleared is good news, but it’s also a warning: the risk of a full stroke is highest in the next few days. That’s why we act today, not next week.
model.why: Names TIA and explains why resolution means urgency, in plain words

model.text: Today? I feel absolutely fine.
I know, and that’s exactly the point — this is the chance to prevent a stroke before it happens. Treatment started early greatly reduces that risk.
model.why: Firm but supportive correction of the minimisation

model.text: Two things now. First, unless there’s a reason not to, take 300 milligrams of aspirin today. Do you have aspirin in the house? If not, I’ll send a prescription to your pharmacy straight away.
model.why: Aspirin 300 mg immediately, having checked for contraindications (NICE NG128)

model.text: I think there’s some in the cupboard.

Check the strength on the pack before you take it — I’ll stay on while you do if you like. Second, I’m referring you now to the stroke team’s TIA clinic, to be seen within 24 hours of when it started. They’ll check your heart rhythm and blood pressure, do bloods and a heart tracing, scan the arteries in your neck, and decide if you need a brain scan.
model.why: Immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset; no ABCD2 delay

model.text: And after that?

They’ll usually start a blood-thinning tablet for the long term, a strong cholesterol tablet, and tighten up your blood pressure. If they find an irregular heartbeat, the treatment changes to an anticoagulant. And staying off cigarettes, as you have, really helps.
Fine. I’ll drive over when they ring.

This is the part you may not like: you must not drive for at least a month after a TIA. That’s the DVLA rule, not just my advice. If you’ve fully recovered at a month you don’t have to tell the DVLA, but if you have another episode the rules become stricter. If you ever drive a bus or lorry, tell me, because then you must stop and inform the DVLA. Could someone else take you to the clinic?
model.why: Correct DVLA Group 1 and Group 2 rules; advice documented

model.text: I’ll sort out a lift. I didn’t know that about driving.

If any weakness, face droop, slurred speech or loss of vision comes back, even for a few minutes, call 999 straight away — don’t wait for the clinic, and don’t wait to see if it passes. Could you tell me back what you’re going to do today?
Aspirin 300 now. Wait for the stroke clinic to ring today. No driving for a month. 999 if it comes back.

Exactly right. If you haven’t heard from the clinic by this afternoon, ring the surgery and we’ll chase it. I’ll record our conversation, including the driving advice, and see you after the clinic to carry on the prevention. Thank your wife for me.
model.why: Closes the loop on the referral and documents the plan

model.text: I will. Thank you — I was going to ignore it.

social.t: Men of his age often delay care after transient symptoms. The family member who prompted attendance is an ally — involve them in transport, aspirin and 999 advice if he agrees.
He cannot drive to the TIA clinic. Check how he will get there today; do not let transport become the reason for delay.

legal.t: Must not drive for 1 month after a TIA. No need to notify if fully recovered at 1 month with no residual deficit. After multiple TIAs, the 1-month exclusion applies after each episode; notify DVLA where the current guidance requires (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
Bus, coach or lorry licence: stop driving and notify DVLA; relicensing requires 1 year and meeting the functional standards (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017): the doctor explains the effect on driving and the patient’s duty to inform the DVLA where required, and documents the advice.
Examination that video cannot provide must be arranged, not assumed. Record which findings were observed on screen and which were deferred to the TIA clinic.

community.t: Stroke Association information on TIA and stroke prevention; NHS Smokefree support if he ever needs help staying stopped.

redFlags: Symptoms persisting or returning now — 999, not the TIA clinic
Already on an anticoagulant or bleeding risk — no aspirin; discuss with the TIA service
Monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax), palpitations suggesting AF, more than one episode
psychosocial: Attended only because his wife insisted
Hidden fear of stroke behind ‘no harm done’
ice: Idea: it resolved, so no harm done
Concern: unspoken fear it was a stroke
Expectation: to be told he can ignore it

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected TIA (anterior circulation: right arm weakness with speech disturbance, fully resolved after about 30 minutes) in a 69-year-old with hypertension and a smoking history. Mimics considered but the default is TIA (NICE NG128).
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A blood vessel to your brain was briefly blocked, then cleared. It’s called a mini-stroke. It’s a warning that a bigger stroke could follow, especially in the next few days — and treatment now can stop that happening.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped it was nothing because it passed. I understand — but the fact it passed is our chance to prevent a stroke.”
management.psychosocial: Credit his wife; arrange someone else to drive him; keep the tone firm but kind, not frightening.
sharedPlan: Aspirin 300 mg now unless contraindicated (NICE NG128)
Immediate referral to be seen by a stroke specialist within 24 hours of onset; no scoring-based delay
Must not drive for at least 1 month (DVLA Group 1); Group 2 stop and notify; documented
Specialist-led secondary prevention continued in practice: antiplatelet or anticoagulant if AF, atorvastatin, BP target, smoking status
safetyNet: 999 immediately if any weakness, face droop, speech or vision change returns, even briefly
Ring the surgery if the TIA clinic has not called today; GP review after clinic

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by reassurance. The candidate who is comforted by full recovery, or who lets the patient’s calm set the pace, misses the whole point of a TIA.

items.fail: “It’s resolved — let’s do some bloods and review next week.”
items.why: The stroke risk is highest in the first days; NICE NG128 wants specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset.
items.fix: Refer immediately and make sure he is seen today.

items.fail: Using an ABCD2 score to decide the referral can wait.
items.why: NICE NG128 advises against scoring systems to set urgency.
items.fix: Treat every suspected TIA as urgent.

items.fail: Advising aspirin without asking about anticoagulants or aspirin allergy.
items.why: Aspirin is contraindicated in some patients and anticoagulated patients need specialist advice.
items.fix: Ask first, then give 300 mg immediately if safe.

items.fail: Saying “avoid driving for a bit” or giving the Group 2 rule to a car driver.
items.why: The DVLA rules are specific and the advice must be documented.
items.fix: Group 1: 1 month, notify only if not fully recovered or multiple TIAs; Group 2: stop, notify, 1 year.

items.fail: Scolding him for waiting a day, or frightening him into agreement.
items.why: Fear or blame reduces engagement with long-term prevention.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear, credit his wife, and present the plan as prevention.

items.fail: Claiming to check pulse, BP or carotids over video.
items.why: Examiners mark down findings that cannot be obtained remotely.
items.fix: Observe what you can, and state that the TIA clinic will examine him today.

items.why: Recurrence needs 999, not a GP appointment.
items.fix: Name the symptoms, say 999, and check with teach-back.

timeMap.d: Check the video set-up. Let him say ‘no harm done’ in full, and thank the wife for pushing him.
Onset, side, speech type, full resolution, vision, mimics, previous episodes, palpitations, anticoagulants and aspirin allergy. Observe speech, face and arm drift on screen.
Ask what he thought while it was happening — the fear of stroke usually surfaces.
TIA as a warning; aspirin 300 mg now; refer to be seen within 24 hours of onset; prevention outline; no driving for a month.
999 if symptoms return; chase if no call today; teach-back; document the driving advice.

wordPics.fail: Reassured because it resolved; books a routine appointment or bloods; uses an ABCD2 score to justify waiting; forgets aspirin or gives it without asking about anticoagulants; claims to examine him over video; never mentions driving.
wordPics.pass: Recognises a suspected TIA; gives aspirin 300 mg; refers to be seen within 24 hours; says he must not drive; gives 999 advice for recurrence.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: surfaces his fear of stroke and handles the minimisation without lecturing; is honest about what video cannot assess; gets the DVLA detail right for Group 1 and Group 2; outlines the prevention package in plain words; closes the loop on the referral; teach-back; he leaves grateful his wife pushed him.

avoid.dont: “Well, it’s all gone now, so that’s good news.”
avoid.instead: “It clearing up is good, but it’s also a warning — the next few days are when a stroke is most likely, so we act today.”
avoid.why: Reassurance from recovery is the exact error NICE NG128 is designed to prevent.

avoid.dont: “Your ABCD2 score is low, so the clinic can see you next week.”
avoid.instead: “I’m referring you now to be seen within 24 hours.”
avoid.why: NICE NG128 advises against scoring systems to set urgency; every suspected TIA is seen within 24 hours.

avoid.dont: “You should probably avoid driving for a bit.”
avoid.instead: “You must not drive for at least a month — that’s the DVLA rule.”
avoid.why: Vague advice is unsafe and does not meet the duty to advise and document.

Your speech sounds clear to me now, and your face looks even on the screen. Could you hold both arms straight out in front of you with your eyes closed for ten seconds? … That looks steady. I can’t check your pulse or blood pressure over video, so the clinic will do that today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses what video allows and names what it cannot do

SCA_MODELS.text: Right.
Have you had anything like this before? Any fluttering or racing heartbeat? And do you take any blood thinners, or have any problem with aspirin or bleeding?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks about previous episodes, symptoms of AF and aspirin contraindications

SCA_MODELS.text: Nothing like that. Just my blood pressure tablets.
You said ‘no harm done’. What went through your mind while it was happening?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the fear behind the minimisation

SCA_MODELS.text: (pause) I suppose I thought it was a stroke. Then it went, so I told myself I’d imagined it.
That must have been frightening, and it’s very human to want it to be nothing. Thank you for telling me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the unspoken fear with empathy

SCA_MODELS.text: I think this was a TIA — a mini-stroke. A blood vessel to the brain was briefly blocked, then cleared. The fact it cleared is good news, but it’s also a warning: the risk of a full stroke is highest in the next few days. That’s why we act today, not next week.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names TIA and explains why resolution means urgency, in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: Today? I feel absolutely fine.
I know, and that’s exactly the point — this is the chance to prevent a stroke before it happens. Treatment started early greatly reduces that risk.
SCA_MODELS.why: Firm but supportive correction of the minimisation

SCA_MODELS.text: Two things now. First, unless there’s a reason not to, take 300 milligrams of aspirin today. Do you have aspirin in the house? If not, I’ll send a prescription to your pharmacy straight away.
SCA_MODELS.why: Aspirin 300 mg immediately, having checked for contraindications (NICE NG128)

SCA_MODELS.text: I think there’s some in the cupboard.

Check the strength on the pack before you take it — I’ll stay on while you do if you like. Second, I’m referring you now to the stroke team’s TIA clinic, to be seen within 24 hours of when it started. They’ll check your heart rhythm and blood pressure, do bloods and a heart tracing, scan the arteries in your neck, and decide if you need a brain scan.
SCA_MODELS.why: Immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset; no ABCD2 delay

SCA_MODELS.text: And after that?

They’ll usually start a blood-thinning tablet for the long term, a strong cholesterol tablet, and tighten up your blood pressure. If they find an irregular heartbeat, the treatment changes to an anticoagulant. And staying off cigarettes, as you have, really helps.
Fine. I’ll drive over when they ring.

This is the part you may not like: you must not drive for at least a month after a TIA. That’s the DVLA rule, not just my advice. If you’ve fully recovered at a month you don’t have to tell the DVLA, but if you have another episode the rules become stricter. If you ever drive a bus or lorry, tell me, because then you must stop and inform the DVLA. Could someone else take you to the clinic?
SCA_MODELS.why: Correct DVLA Group 1 and Group 2 rules; advice documented

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll sort out a lift. I didn’t know that about driving.

If any weakness, face droop, slurred speech or loss of vision comes back, even for a few minutes, call 999 straight away — don’t wait for the clinic, and don’t wait to see if it passes. Could you tell me back what you’re going to do today?
Aspirin 300 now. Wait for the stroke clinic to ring today. No driving for a month. 999 if it comes back.

Exactly right. If you haven’t heard from the clinic by this afternoon, ring the surgery and we’ll chase it. I’ll record our conversation, including the driving advice, and see you after the clinic to carry on the prevention. Thank your wife for me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes the loop on the referral and documents the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: I will. Thank you — I was going to ignore it.

SCA_STEM.name: Bernard Cole
meds: Antihypertensive treatment as on repeat list — check for any anticoagulant or antiplatelet before advising aspirin
SCA_STEM.recent: Yesterday: right arm weakness and slurred speech for about 30 minutes, fully resolved. Attending at his wife’s insistence. No contact about this episode before today.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation. “My wife made me book — it’s passed now, so no harm done?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG128 (stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s: diagnosis and initial management, 2019, updated 2022) · [2] National Clinical Guideline for Stroke for the UK and Ireland (ICSWP, 2023) · [3] NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · [4] NICE NG196 (atrial fibrillation, 2021) · [5] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition) · [6] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Sudden right arm weakness with slurred speech lasting about 30 minutes and fully resolving, in a 69-year-old hypertensive ex-smoker, is a suspected TIA until a specialist says otherwise. Recovery is the reason to act, not a reason to relax: the stroke risk is highest in the first days. The GP’s job is aspirin 300 mg now unless contraindicated, a same-day referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset, clear no-driving advice and a firm 999 safety net.

points.t: A sudden focal deficit (unilateral weakness, speech disturbance, facial droop, monocular visual loss) that fully resolves is a suspected TIA. Arm weakness plus dysarthria or dysphasia points to the anterior circulation. Mimics — hypoglycaemia, focal seizure with Todd’s paresis, migraine aura, syncope — are considered, but the default is to treat as TIA [1].

NICE NG128 [1]: offer aspirin 300 mg immediately to people with suspected TIA unless contraindicated. If he already takes an anticoagulant, or has a bleeding disorder or aspirin hypersensitivity, do not give it and discuss with the TIA service [1].

NICE NG128 [1]: refer immediately to be seen by a stroke specialist within 24 hours of symptom onset. If the TIA was more than a week ago, the target is within 7 days. NG128 says do not use scoring systems such as ABCD2 to decide urgency — every suspected TIA gets the urgent route. Symptoms that return and persist mean 999, not the clinic.

NICE NG128 [1]: do not offer CT brain to people with suspected TIA unless an alternative diagnosis that CT could detect is suspected. The specialist decides on MRI (diffusion-weighted) and arranges urgent carotid imaging. Carotid endarterectomy is considered for 50–99% symptomatic stenosis (NASCET), ideally within a week of onset.

Delivered by the TIA service and continued in general practice: long-term clopidogrel in most people, with short specialist-started dual antiplatelet therapy for selected high-risk TIA [2]; anticoagulation instead if AF is found (NICE NG196 [4]); atorvastatin 80 mg unless there is a reason for a lower dose (NICE NG238 [3]); blood pressure target of systolic below 130 mmHg [2]; staying off tobacco; diabetes and lipid checks.

DVLA [5]: Group 1 (car, motorcycle) — must not drive for 1 month. No need to notify DVLA if fully recovered at 1 month with no residual deficit. After multiple TIAs, the 1-month exclusion applies after each episode; notify DVLA where the current guidance requires. Group 2 (bus, coach, lorry): stop driving and notify; relicensing needs 1 year. Record the advice in the notes [6].

On video you can watch speech and face and ask about symptoms, but you cannot take a blood pressure, feel the pulse for AF or listen for a bruit. Say so, and make sure the TIA clinic does the examination, ECG and bloods the same day.
‘It’s passed, so no harm done’ is a common reason for dangerous delay. Name it kindly, credit the person who pushed him to come, and explain that the warning is the chance to prevent a stroke.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let him give the full story and his ‘no harm done’ view before questioning.
Acknowledged the wife’s role; explored his fear of stroke; asked about driving and who could take him to clinic.
Picked up ‘it’s passed’ as minimisation and the hidden fear behind it; explored rather than argued.
Idea: resolved means harmless. Concern: unspoken fear of stroke. Expectation: permission to ignore it.
Used video to observe speech, face and arm drift; stated that BP, pulse, bruits, ECG and bloods need the TIA clinic today.
Considered mimics (hypoglycaemia, seizure, migraine aura, syncope) and amaurosis fugax; kept TIA as the working diagnosis.
Checked for persisting deficit (999 if present) and for anticoagulant, bleeding risk and aspirin allergy.
Suspected anterior-circulation TIA; explained as a mini-stroke and a warning with the highest risk in the next few days.
Aspirin 300 mg now; immediate referral to be seen within 24 hours of onset; no ABCD2 triage; outlined clopidogrel, statin, BP and AF plan.
Linked hypertension and smoking history to prevention; AF to be sought; driving advice with DVLA rules documented.
999 for any recurrence; chase the clinic if no call today; review after clinic; teach-back.

social.t: Men of his age often delay care after transient symptoms. The family member who prompted attendance is an ally — involve them in transport, aspirin and 999 advice if he agrees.
He cannot drive to the TIA clinic. Check how he will get there today; do not let transport become the reason for delay.

legal.t: Must not drive for 1 month after a TIA. No need to notify if fully recovered at 1 month with no residual deficit. After multiple TIAs, the 1-month exclusion applies after each episode; notify DVLA where the current guidance requires (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
Bus, coach or lorry licence: stop driving and notify DVLA; relicensing requires 1 year and meeting the functional standards (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA or DVA (2017): the doctor explains the effect on driving and the patient’s duty to inform the DVLA where required, and documents the advice.
Examination that video cannot provide must be arranged, not assumed. Record which findings were observed on screen and which were deferred to the TIA clinic.

community.t: Stroke Association information on TIA and stroke prevention; NHS Smokefree support if he ever needs help staying stopped.

redFlags: Symptoms persisting or returning now — 999, not the TIA clinic
Already on an anticoagulant or bleeding risk — no aspirin; discuss with the TIA service
Monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax), palpitations suggesting AF, more than one episode
psychosocial: Attended only because his wife insisted
Hidden fear of stroke behind ‘no harm done’
ice: Idea: it resolved, so no harm done
Concern: unspoken fear it was a stroke
Expectation: to be told he can ignore it

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected TIA (anterior circulation: right arm weakness with speech disturbance, fully resolved after about 30 minutes) in a 69-year-old with hypertension and a smoking history. Mimics considered but the default is TIA (NICE NG128).
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A blood vessel to your brain was briefly blocked, then cleared. It’s called a mini-stroke. It’s a warning that a bigger stroke could follow, especially in the next few days — and treatment now can stop that happening.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped it was nothing because it passed. I understand — but the fact it passed is our chance to prevent a stroke.”
management.psychosocial: Credit his wife; arrange someone else to drive him; keep the tone firm but kind, not frightening.
sharedPlan: Aspirin 300 mg now unless contraindicated (NICE NG128)
Immediate referral to be seen by a stroke specialist within 24 hours of onset; no scoring-based delay
Must not drive for at least 1 month (DVLA Group 1); Group 2 stop and notify; documented
Specialist-led secondary prevention continued in practice: antiplatelet or anticoagulant if AF, atorvastatin, BP target, smoking status
safetyNet: 999 immediately if any weakness, face droop, speech or vision change returns, even briefly
Ring the surgery if the TIA clinic has not called today; GP review after clinic

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by reassurance. The candidate who is comforted by full recovery, or who lets the patient’s calm set the pace, misses the whole point of a TIA.

items.fail: “It’s resolved — let’s do some bloods and review next week.”
items.why: The stroke risk is highest in the first days; NICE NG128 wants specialist assessment within 24 hours of onset.
items.fix: Refer immediately and make sure he is seen today.

items.fail: Using an ABCD2 score to decide the referral can wait.
items.why: NICE NG128 advises against scoring systems to set urgency.
items.fix: Treat every suspected TIA as urgent.

items.fail: Advising aspirin without asking about anticoagulants or aspirin allergy.
items.why: Aspirin is contraindicated in some patients and anticoagulated patients need specialist advice.
items.fix: Ask first, then give 300 mg immediately if safe.

items.fail: Saying “avoid driving for a bit” or giving the Group 2 rule to a car driver.
items.why: The DVLA rules are specific and the advice must be documented.
items.fix: Group 1: 1 month, notify only if not fully recovered or multiple TIAs; Group 2: stop, notify, 1 year.

items.fail: Scolding him for waiting a day, or frightening him into agreement.
items.why: Fear or blame reduces engagement with long-term prevention.
items.fix: Acknowledge the fear, credit his wife, and present the plan as prevention.

items.fail: Claiming to check pulse, BP or carotids over video.
items.why: Examiners mark down findings that cannot be obtained remotely.
items.fix: Observe what you can, and state that the TIA clinic will examine him today.

items.why: Recurrence needs 999, not a GP appointment.
items.fix: Name the symptoms, say 999, and check with teach-back.
